description_full: RTX Corporation, an aerospace and defense company, provides systems and services for commercial, military, and government customers worldwide. It operates through three segments: Collins Aerospace (Collins), Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon. The Collins segment offers aerospace and defense products, and aftermarket services for civil and military aircraft manufacturers and commercial airlines, as well as regional, business, and general aviation, defense, and commercial space operations. This segment designs, manufactures, and supplies electric power generation and management and distribution, environmental control, flight control, air data and aircraft sensing, engine control, and engine nacelle systems, as well as engine components; cabin interiors, including seating, oxygen, food and beverage preparation, storage and galley, lavatory, and wastewater management systems; connected aviation solutions and services; and systems solutions for connected battlespace, test and training range systems, crew escape systems, and simulation and training. It also provides spare parts, overhaul and repair, engineering and technical support, training and fleet management solutions, and asset and information management services. The Pratt & Whitney segment supplies aircraft engines for commercial, military, business jet, and general aviation customers; and produces, sells, and services military and commercial auxiliary power units, as well as offers fleet management and aftermarket maintenance, repair, and overhaul services. The Raytheon segment provides defensive and offensive threat detection, tracking, and mitigation capabilities for government and commercial customers. This segment offers sensors, mission orchestration and satellite control products, and software. The company was formerly known as Raytheon Technologies Corporation and changed its name to RTX Corporation in July 2023. RTX Corporation was incorporated in 1934 and is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia.

financial_summary: RTX Corporation is a mega-cap industrials business with a $255.8B market cap on $88.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $7.9B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.57× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.0×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.95x).
It accounts for 2.3% of sector revenue and 2.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 14% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $811.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 52% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 49% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $150 (margin of safety -26%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $111 to $209 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 30.8 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 17.1 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 32.2 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 32% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $228 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.57x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.9x net debt to EBITDA ($8.2B of cash against $34.5B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.7% over 3 years, 9.4% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 0.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 25.6% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.56 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 3.0x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 16%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (3.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 82%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $21.7M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.4% (0.0% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 63 consecutive years, raising it 5.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 180,000 employees, each generates about $492K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 3.3% a year.
That works out to $44K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.2M (15x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
